nameStory: The Triangulate Combfoot gets its name from the distinctive triangle-shaped pattern that decorates the top of its abdomen, like a geometric tattoo. The 'combfoot' part refers to the special comb-like bristles on their hind legs that help them handle their sticky silk when building webs. It's also sometimes called the 'checkered cobweb weaver' because those triangular markings can look like a checkerboard pattern from certain angles.
description: The Triangulate Combfoot is a small, brownish spider that's probably living closer to you than you think. These compact spiders are about the size of a small pea, with females slightly larger than males. Their most striking feature is the zigzag or triangular pattern running down their rounded abdomen, which looks like chevrons or arrowheads pointing toward their head. They're members of the 'false widow' family, related to black widows but much less dangerous.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive triangular or zigzag pattern on top of the abdomen - it's usually cream, yellow, or light brown against a darker background, creating a chevron effect that's unmistakable once you see it

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The abdomen is noticeably round and bulbous, like a small marble, while the front section (cephalothorax) is much smaller and darker, giving the spider a distinctive two-part silhouette

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates irregular, messy-looking cobwebs with sticky capture threads - not the classic spiral orb web, but rather a tangled 3D structure that feels sticky to the touch if you accidentally walk into it

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females reach about 1/4 inch in body length (not counting legs), roughly the size of a small pea, while males are noticeably smaller at about 1/8 inch

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often hangs upside down in the center or corner of their web, and when disturbed, they may drop down on a silk line or curl up into a tight ball

habitat: These adaptable spiders thrive around human structures throughout New England, making their homes in garages, sheds, basements, window frames, and under eaves. You'll often find them in corners where walls meet ceilings, around outdoor light fixtures, or in cluttered areas like woodpiles and garden tools. They prefer dry, sheltered spots and are especially common in suburban and urban areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and begin building new webs. This is when you're most likely to spot the distinctive triangular markings as they become active again.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time with adults readily visible in their webs. Mating occurs and females can be seen guarding round, papery egg sacs that feel like tiny balloons.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active and visible, with newly matured spiders establishing territories. Late fall brings egg-laying activity before winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Most retreat to protected crevices and become inactive, though in heated buildings like basements and garages, some may remain active year-round.

funFact: Despite being called a 'false widow,' the Triangulate Combfoot is actually more closely related to the deadly black widow than most people realize - they're in the same family and even share some of the same web-building techniques, but evolution made them harmless to humans while keeping the architectural skills!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with actual black widows, but triangulate combfoots lack the glossy black coloration and red hourglass marking. Remember: triangles on top = harmless combfoot, red hourglass underneath = widow spider. The triangular pattern is your safety signal.
contextualKnowledge: The 'false widow' name can be misleading - it doesn't mean they're pretending to be widows, but rather that early naturalists grouped them with widow spiders before understanding they're much less dangerous. While they can bite if handled roughly, their bite is typically no worse than a mosquito bite for most people.
compareHints: Among New England's false widows, the Triangulate Combfoot is the only one with clear triangular markings on the abdomen. The False Black Widow is much larger and darker, while the Boreal Combfoot lacks distinct patterns. The White-spotted False Widow has white spots rather than triangular chevrons, making the triangulate pattern your best field mark for this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's false widow spiders, the Boreal Combfoot is most similar to the False Black Widow but is typically smaller and lacks the distinctive glossy, jet-black coloration.

Among its Steatoda relatives in New England, the False Black Widow is the largest and darkest, lacking the distinctive white triangular markings of the Triangulate Combfoot or the white spots of the White-spotted False Widow.

Among its false widow relatives in New England, the White-spotted False Widow is distinguished by its clear white markings, while the Triangulate Combfoot has chevron or zigzag patterns, and the False Black Widow is usually larger and darker with less distinct markings.

Among New England's false widows, the Rabbit Hutch Spider is distinguished by its brownish coloration and the specific pale line pattern on its abdomen - the broken center line plus the cross-line create a unique signature.
The Noble False Widow is the largest and most robust of the false widow species, with a more distinctly bulbous abdomen than the Triangulate Combfoot or False Black Widow.
